# Exact parallel-chord distributions in an arbitrary simplex direction

This is a proved ordinary geometric input for the higher-dimensional
roof route. It is not a mixed-integer center theorem.

## 1. Simplex, direction, and the transverse measure

Let d>=2, m=d+1, and let a_0,...,a_d span R^d with the sole
linear dependence sum_i a_i=0. Assume

    T={x:a_i.x<=1 for every i}

is a bounded full-dimensional simplex, of volume V. Choose a direction
e with a_0.e=1, and use the longitudinal coordinate t=a_0.x.
Each line parallel to e has unique representation x=y+t e, with
y in ker(a_0). Write ell(y) for the length of its t interval in T,
zero for an empty section. The exact transverse measure is

    dnu(y)=dH_(d-1)(y)/||a_0||,

so ordinary coarea, or the determinant of x=y+t e, gives

    V=integral ell(y)dnu(y).

Put

    sigma=sum_i(a_i.e)_+ >=1,
    L=m/sigma,
    P=V d/L=V d sigma/m.

The inequality sigma>=1 uses the actual term a_0.e=1.

## 2. A translated homothety describes every directional overlap

For s>=0,

    T intersect (T-s e)
       ={x:a_i.x<=1-s(a_i.e)_+ for all i}.           (1)

For 0<=s<=L, put rho=1-s sigma/m. The numbers

    -s(a_i.e)_+ +s sigma/m

sum to zero, so there is a unique vector v_s having those scalar
products with the a_i. Existence and uniqueness follow because the
map x -> (a_i.x)_i is an isomorphism onto the d-dimensional
coordinate hyperplane in R^m whose coordinate sum is zero. Thus (1) is
exactly v_s+rho T. At s=L it is a point. For s>L it is empty,
because summing its m inequalities gives 0<=m-s sigma<0.
Consequently

    |T intersect (T-s e)|=V(1-s/L)^d   (0<=s<=L),
                            0          (s>=L).       (2)

On each parallel line the overlap has length (ell-s)_+. Therefore

    integral(ell-s)_+ dnu=V(1-s/L)^d.               (3)

Its right derivative is -nu{ell>s}, by dominated convergence:
the difference quotient is bounded by1 on the finite transverse
projection of T. Differentiating (3) gives the exact chord tail

    nu{ell>s}=P(1-s/L)^(d-1),    0<=s<L.            (4)

The same formula from the left shows that ell has no atom at an
interior positive level. The atom at L also vanishes because d>=2
and the right side tends to zero as s increases to L. In particular
the total transverse projection measure is P.

The projection of T is a full-dimensional convex body in ker(a_0),
and its boundary has (d-1)-measure zero. Every interior projection
point has ell>0. Thus nu{ell>0}=nu(pi_e T), as used here.

The distribution of positive ell under nu consequently has density

    [P(d-1)/L](1-v/L)^(d-2) dv, 0<v<L.             (5)

This is an exact distribution identity, including directions that
do not join the lowest vertex to the opposite facet. Directional
dependence occurs only through sigma.

## 3. The least transverse support needed for a prescribed subbody volume

Let B subset T be a convex body, with volume b in (0,V]. Write
ell_B for its t-section lengths. Then 0<=ell_B<=ell. For every
measurable transverse set E supporting ell_B,

    b<=integral_E ell dnu.

The maximum integral of ell on a prescribed nu-measure is obtained
on its upper level set. This follows directly from the signed
threshold comparison: if E and {ell>=v_0} have the same measure,
the integral of (1_{ell>=v_0}-1_E)(ell-v_0) is nonnegative.
Fractional selectors obey the identical argument, so no existence
of a maximizing B is required.

Let eta in (0,1] be the unique solution

    b/V=d eta^(d-1)-(d-1)eta^d.                     (6)

The right side increases strictly from0 to1 on (0,1), since its
derivative is d(d-1)eta^(d-2)(1-eta)>0. Formula(5), integrated
above v_0=L(1-eta), gives

    nu{ell>=v_0}=P eta^(d-1),
    integral_{ell>=v_0}ell dnu
        =V[d eta^(d-1)-(d-1)eta^d]=b.              (7)

Hence the actual transverse projection of B has measure at least

    nu(pi_e B)>=P eta^(d-1).                       (8)

For b=V, the same result follows from ell_B=ell almost everywhere;
both sides in (8) equal P. This handles the endpoint without an
unjustified strict-threshold choice.

The bound (8) is sharp among actual convex subbodies, for every e.
The chord length ell is concave on pi_e T by interpolation of its
interval sections. Thus E={ell>=v_0} is convex. The body
B=T intersect pi_e^(-1)(E) has exactly the volume and projection
measure in (7). For 0<b<V, this E has positive measure and hence
relative interior, while its chord lengths are positive; B is full
dimensional. At b=V take B=T. This is a standalone sharpness claim
for the projection bound, not for the roof relaxation (9).

## 4. An all-dimensional roof bound

Suppose h>d and put H=h+1>m. In the same longitudinal coordinate,
T has range [-d,1]. Let [L_B(y),U_B(y)] be the actual t sections
of B. Define its positive roof cost

    R_e(B,h)=integral_(pi_e B)[h+U_B(y)]dnu(y).

Since L_B>=-d,

    h+U_B=(U_B-L_B)+(h+L_B)
           >=ell_B+(H-m).

Using (8) yields the proved bound

    R_e(B,h)>=b+(H-m)P eta^(d-1)
             >=b+(H-m)(Vd/m)eta^(d-1).             (9)

The simpler pointwise estimate, valid without simplex chord data,
is R_e>=Hb/m. The inequality in (9) improves it because
P eta^(d-1)>=b/L>=b/m. In dimension2 it is weaker than the
sharp slope-resolved roof bound already proved separately; it is
not being represented as the sharp higher-dimensional analogue.

If an actual segment S subset A joins t extrema l<-1<h and has
direction e as above, it has fixed transverse coordinate y_A. The
sections of S+B occur at y_A+y; translation invariance of nu and
B subset T give

    |(S+B) intersect {t>=0}|=R_e(B,h).

Indeed every section is [l+L_B,h+U_B], with endpoints of opposite
sign. Thus if (A+B)/2 subset K,

    2^d |K intersect {t>=0}|>=R_e(B,h).             (10)

Every transformation and measure factor in this input is explicit.
No midpoint that leaves the integer base is used: (10) concerns
one already compatible pair of continuous endpoint fibers. The
factor2^d is retained exactly, and no OC constant follows from
this input alone.
